property.name: Pages
property.value: A stone at the mouth of the cleft, and the wood behind you is the last of it. "THE RIVEN PASS. DEEPDELVE BEYOND. NO CARTS AFTER DARK." Somebody has scratched out the last four words and written nothing in their place.

property.name: Pages
property.value: A board under the office eave, ruled into two columns in a careful hand. On the left, every party that has gone up to the mouth, with the date and the number in it. On the right, the same parties coming back down. The left column runs to the bottom of the board and continues on a second sheet nailed under it. The right column stops two thirds of the way.

property.name: Pages
property.value: The winding gear stands over the adit, greased and sound and perfectly still. The drum is full of rope. Nobody has taken it down, and nobody will: taking it down would be saying out loud what everybody here already knows.

property.name: Pages
property.value: A cart at the sorting floor with ore still in it, and a chalk mark on the side giving the date it was filled. It is the date of the feast. Rain has been on the chalk and the numbers have run, but they are still the numbers.␟The ore cart stood where the narrow track widened before the mouth of Deepdelve. Its wheels had long ago sunk a finger's depth into the earth, and no one had troubled to move it since the lower shafts flooded some fifteen winters before. The timber sides were silvered by weather, split where summer heat had opened the grain, and the iron bands carried more rust than black. Someone had taken to using its broad side as a writing board, for chalk held well enough against the old oak until rain came to fetch it away. Most of the writing had already begun to run. White streaks wandered down the timber where the weather had carried the letters with it, leaving only broken words and pale ghosts of numbers. Yet beneath the shelter of the cart's warped overhang enough remained to be read.␟Feast Day. Started work late. The bells from Ashwold carried farther than usual this morning. Old Gerth said the damp air does that. I know little enough about air, but I know men work slower when feast bells are still ringing in their ears. The upper seam has given us nothing worth hauling these past three days. Too much loose stone. Not enough ore. We spent the morning clearing fallen shale where the old mule track bends toward the cave. Near midday four travellers came along that very road. Not strangers. Village folk. I knew Brann well enough to put a name to him, though we had not shared a drink since the winter the east roof of the forge came down. Toman I knew by his beard before I knew his face. The woman wore a red scarf bright enough to catch the eye even amongst the pines, and the youngest fellow seemed incapable of keeping silence for more than half a minute before another tune escaped between his teeth.␟Brann asked whether the old descent beyond the pit remained passable. I told him it did, though the rains had loosened much of the slope. He asked whether anyone had gone below recently. I answered truthfully that no sensible miner had reason to. He smiled at that, though not because he found it amusing — rather it was the smile of a man who has already chosen his road and asks questions only to satisfy those walking beside him. The younger one laughed. He said there was little use climbing a mountain merely to admire it from outside. Toman answered before I could. 'There are doors best left closed,' he said. The lad replied that every old man says the same thing until someone else opens them. No one argued after that. The woman reached into one of the mule's packs and broke off the heel of yesterday's bread for the beast before they continued. It took the crust gently from her hand. Funny what a man remembers afterwards.␟Rain found us not long after they disappeared amongst the trees. The chalk smears here where the writer must have stopped, for the next lines have been written lower, beneath the shelter of the cart. Toward evening I found an oil flask beside the track. Not dropped. Placed upright against a stone. Empty. Clean enough that it looked newly scrubbed. No miner wastes time cleaning an empty flask. I left it where it stood. When I passed again after the rain eased, it was gone. There were fresh hoofprints leading back toward Ashwold. Only one set. No boot marks beside them. I remained until sunset, listening for voices coming down from the ridge. The mountain gave me only water dripping through broken timbers and, once, something that sounded very much like iron striking stone. It came only three times. Then not again.␟The date was written once more beneath the final line, though the rain had almost carried it away. Whoever returned to the cart after writing this had pressed the last words so firmly that they bit into the timber beneath the chalk: if they come asking whether I saw the four return, tell them I watched until the light was gone. I saw only the mule.

property.name: Pages
property.value: Meltwater with nowhere to go, black because it is deep and because nothing lives in it. The pump takes off the near end and has done for years. Along the far shore, where nobody walks, the stones are laid in a line too straight to have fallen that way.

property.name: Pages
property.value: The turn of the switchback, and the place where anyone climbing it stops to get their breath. That is why the offerings are here and not at the top: a lamp, a folded coat, a child's shoe with the lace still tied. People leave things where they stop, not where they mean to.

property.name: Pages
property.value: A cave amongst the cliffs, and the cold coming out of it is not the cold of the mountain. The timbering at the entrance is old mine work and it stops eight feet in, because eight feet in the passage stops being anything men made. A board is wedged in the rock beside it. "THE ACCOUNT OF THIS PLACE IS KEPT BELOW. WE DO NOT KEEP IT."

property.name: Pages
property.value: A fire, banked and fed, on the shelf outside the mouth. Somebody has kept it going for a long while — the ash under it is a foot deep. It is not there to cook on and it is not there for warmth. It is there so that anything coming out has to come out past a light.

property.name: Pages
property.value: Eighteen bunks, and the blankets on eleven of them are folded the way a man folds a blanket when he is coming back to it. Nobody has moved them. The cook still lays eighteen places, which the captain has told her twice to stop doing.
